baer-heitev/1:א: (א) And then. The Levush wrote that one who lit Shabbat first and did not accept Shabbat with intent that he could light afterward — see there. The Taz disagrees and wrote that he cannot light, since for us there is a widespread custom that a woman who lights the Shabbat candle accepts Shabbat upon herself and is forbidden in melacha, while other household members are still permitted; therefore a man who lights the Shabbat candle and forgot to light Chanukah may not light Chanukah afterward, but should have one of his household members light — see there. It appears to me that for a woman who lights, since the custom is that she accepts Shabbat with her lighting as written in siman 263 seif 10, therefore according to all she should not light Chanukah again but tell another to light. Magen Avraham — see there.
baer-heitev/1:ב: (ב) Great. Specifically after plag haMincha. Bach:
beer-hagolah/1:א: (א) Tur in the name of Baal HaHalachot Gedolot
beer-hagolah/1:ב: (ב) And he concluded there: since one cannot be involved in another matter, thought renders the mitzvah fit, etc.
machatzit-hashekel/1:_: (s.k. 1) On erev Shabbat etc. It appears to me that for a woman who lights, since the custom etc. But for a man there is no custom, as Magen Avraham wrote above siman 263 s.k. 18; therefore b'dieved he agrees with the Levush, not as the Taz wrote here that even for a man if he lit Shabbat it is forbidden to light Chanukah. See section 476 in the name of Bach that even a man who already lit Chanukah may light and recite the blessing for a woman. See there whether she must stand next to him:
magen-avraham/1:א: (א) On erev Shabbat etc. And b'dieved if he lit Shabbat and did not accept Shabbat in his thought he may light afterward (Levush). It appears to me that for a woman who lights, since the custom is that she accepts Shabbat with her lighting as written in siman 263 seif 10, therefore she should not light Chanukah again but tell another to light [see section 476]:
magen-avraham/1:ב: (ב) While the day is still great. Because one cannot be involved in another matter, thought renders the mitzvah fit [Terumat HaDeshen]; it appears to me specifically after plag haMincha as written in siman 472, and so in Bach:
mechaber/1:main: On erev Shabbat one lights the Chanukah candle first and then the Shabbat candle. {Rama: And he blesses on them as on a weekday, even though they light while the day is still great [Terumat HaDeshen siman 102]}:
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (א) Chanukah candle first — in order to satisfy the view of the Yesh Omrim who hold that if one lights Shabbat first he accepts Shabbat and melacha becomes forbidden for him; but most poskim disagree and hold that acceptance of Shabbat is not dependent on lighting the candle; therefore if he lit Shabbat and did not accept Shabbat in his thought he may light afterward. This is for a man who lights; but a woman who lights, since the custom is that she presumably accepts Shabbat with her lighting, therefore she should not light Chanukah again but tell another to light, and he will bless she'asah nissim to light on her behalf; but the blessing she'asah nissim and likewise shehecheyanu on the first day she may recite herself:
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (ב) While the day is still great — specifically after plag haMincha, which is an hour and a quarter before night as written at the beginning of siman 472. We already wrote in the name of the Acharonim that one must put enough oil that it burns half an hour after nightfall; the same for one who lights candles. If he does not have so much oil and large candles, he should see to it that at least one of them burns this amount. The Acharonim wrote that it is proper l'chatchila to pray Mincha first and then light:
turei-zahav/1:_: Chanukah first. For if one lights Shabbat first he accepts Shabbat and melacha becomes forbidden for him — so in Beit HaGadol. The Tosafot disagree and hold that acceptance of Shabbat is not dependent on lighting the candle; and for us there is a widespread custom that a woman who lights the Shabbat candle accepts Shabbat upon herself and is forbidden in melacha, while other household members are still permitted; therefore a man who lights Shabbat and forgot Chanukah may not light Chanukah afterward but should have one of his household light.
